params.text: Two hyperboloids, aplanatic · the design of nearly every large research telescope · 2D geometric interpretation

### Giving up a perfect axis to buy a usable field
Make the primary a **parabola** (k = -1) with the hyperbolic secondary that shares its focus (k = -2.609467) and
this becomes a classical Cassegrain: exactly stigmatic on the axis, spot **4.5e-7 mm**. Tilt it a tenth of a degree
and that becomes **5.0e-3 mm**, one-sided — **coma**, the aberration that confines a classical Cassegrain to a
narrow field.

The Ritchey–Chrétien makes **both** mirrors hyperbolic and gives up the exact axis — **5.4e-4 mm**, no longer zero —
to cancel coma across the field: **1.9e-3 mm** at the same tenth of a degree. Hubble, the VLT and Keck are all this
design, because a telescope is judged on the field it can image and not on the single point at its centre.

**Try:** set primary k = -1 and secondary k = -2.609467 for the classical Cassegrain and compare — on axis it gets
*better*, which is the whole point · by 0.3° the two are close again (2.2e-2 against 1.4e-2 mm), because what is
left there is astigmatism, which this design does not claim to correct.

A 2D meridional section: no sagittal plane, so astigmatism and field curvature are not shown as a real instrument
would show them, and nothing here is diffractive — no Airy disc, and none of the ring redistribution the central
obstruction really causes. The secondary blocks the middle of the aperture because it is genuinely in the way.
Signal is a relative sum over this 2D ray section, not transmitted power through a circular pupil, so what the
obstruction costs here is not the fraction a 3D area calculation would give.
